reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
He, C., Amodio, M. et al. introduces TRIM (TCR-RNA Integrating Model), a multimodal conditional variational autoencoder designed to jointly analyze T cell RNA and TCR sequence data. TRIM aims to learn a shared representation of transcriptomic and TCR clonality information, conditioned on key clinical and biological covariates such as patient identity, tumor vs other tissue, and treatment timepoint. The authors apply the model to two datasets: one comprising head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) patients sampled before and after checkpoint inhibition from blood and tumor, and another consisting of a pan-cancer RNA-TCR dataset with tumor and normal-juxta tissue. The model demonstrates predictive capabilities for T cell clonal expansion and transcriptional states, highlighting its potential utility in modeling T cell responses under treatment.
The study is timely and introduces a new approach for integration of these single-cell data modalities. The manuscript is clearly motivated, and the proposed method shows promising results in the field of immunotherapy outcome predictions. However, several aspects of the methodology and evaluation require clarification or expansion. Below, I provide detailed major and minor comments that could strengthen the manuscript.
Major Comments:
• The authors highlight repeatedly that in their analyses, although cells with identical TCRs are very close in gene expression space, gene expression differences between cells with different TCRs is unrelated to TCR similarity. This seems to be in strong contrast to reports showing that the TCR sequence can be predictive of T cell fate such as DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2024.115098, DOI: 10.1101/2025.05.31.657155, DOI: 10.1038/s41587-021-00989-2, DOI: 10.1038/s41590-022-01129-x. This apparent discrepancy needs to at least be extensively discussed, and preferably explained, in the current manuscript.
• What is the rationale for using only the beta chain? Clarifying this choice would help assess how much signal is potentially missed by excluding the alpha chain.
• Why was Hamming distance used for TCR similarity, whereas Levenshtein distance is more commonly adopted in TCR studies? Levenshtein allows exploration of amino acid-level mismatches that Hamming does not.
• Performance on the pan-cancer dataset appears notably more modest than on HNSCC. This suggests potential limitations in generalization, and questions its contribution on a clinical perspective. Perhaps the difference comes from the source of healthy tissue (blood in HNSCC, juxta-tumor in pan-cancer). Can the authors identify another public dataset with blood and tumor (inline with the HNSCC cohort) to evaluate this possibility ?
• Page 10, towards end of last paragraph “When we isolated this subset of genes in our model’s ranking by log fold change, we found that, as expected, the expansion signature genes were more likely to be differentially expressed in clones that the model predicted to expand (Fig. 5a).” : Given that the p value for this test is 0.064, I do not understand why it is described as a positive result.
Minor Comments:
• Consider comparing TCR-derived distances to those in the gene expression PCA space as a control of model latent space structure (and deformation).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The study reported TRIM as a promising tool for predicting T cell states and responses to cancer immunotherapies using peripheral blood measurements. While the initial findings are encouraging and highlight the potential for clinical application, there are several areas that warrant further clarification and expansion to enhance the study's impact and translational relevance.
Major comments:
1. The study would be strengthened by a more in-depth analysis of inter-individual variability in immune responses. Key factors such as age, sex, race, and genetic background are known to significantly impact immune cell behavior and responses to immunotherapy. It remains unclear whether TRIM accounts for these sources of variation or how its predictive performance may differ across diverse patient populations. Including data analysis based on clinicopathological features in the patient cohorts would provide a more comprehensive assessment of TRIM’s potential for equitable application in clinical practice.
2. In this study, the authors applied TRIM to T cells isolated from both blood and tumor biopsies of patients with HNSCC. However, the rationale behind selecting HNSCC as the disease model is not clearly explained.
3. The patient data used to validate the predictive value of TRIM were all derived from relatively less prevalent cancer types, including HNSCC, ESCA, THCA, and UCEC. While these datasets provide initial support for TRIM’s utility, validation in more common and clinically impactful cancer types, such as breast and prostate cancer, would significantly strengthen the generalizability and translational relevance of the findings. Including such high-prevalence cancers for data validation is required to enhance the clinical applicability of the tool.
4. While the study identifies numerous genes and gene signatures through the application of TRIM, there is a lack of in- depth interpretation and biological context provided for these findings. Further analysis and discussion are needed to clarify the functional relevance of these genes, their potential roles in T cell biology or immunotherapy response,
5. It would be great to discuss on how sample size of patients contributes to the predictive power of the TRIM model.
(Remarks on code availability)
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This study takes single cell RNA transcriptomic data and TCR data from blood and tumour and integrates them into a single low dimensional latent variable (coded as a Gaussian of specified mean and variance in a space of predetermined dimension), which can then be decoded so as to produce a generative model of transcriptional state and TCR. It adds to a growing body of literature which addresses integration of multimodal data. The model is used to investigate the relationship between TCR and transcription, and to predict population-level features as well as individual cell expansion in tumour and blood pre-and post- treatment , based on pretreatment blood alone.
I would summarise the most important findings as 1. Transcriptional state of T cells from the same clone are more similar to each other than to other clones, but for non-identical TCRs there is no relationship to transcriptional state. 2. The expansion potential of a TCR can be predicted from its pre-treatment transcriptional state (as shown in the original paper).
I was less convinced by the comparisons between TRIM and other ML approaches to prediction – its hard to directly compare, and to ensure that the other methods have been optimised at hyperparameter level. I was also not completely convinced about the insights into the gene prediction section. Why do the authors think that prediction of genes driving expansion is better or more complete than using the actual differential gene expression profiles for those T cells which expand Is the imposition of similar transcriptional profiles for the same clone somehow reducing the noise in some way?
I wondered why patient id is encoded in the model? Surely id is a totally arbitrary field ? Why does its encoding need learning ?
I am not convinced of the predictive features of the model – leave-one-out prediction from a single data set is not equivalent to validating in an independent cohort, even with the same treatment and/or cancer, let alone more broadly. And, at least to my understanding, the validation in a second data set involved re-learning the model with the second set of data. So its unclear how generalizable the models are.
In summary, the concept of TRIM is elegant and the fact that it is possible to encode the combined TCR/transcription profile in a low dimensional latent Gaussian variable and retain useful information is interesting. I am not convinced that the findings from application of the model so far substantially advance the field.
(Remarks on code availability)
I did not have time to install adn test teh code on an HPC.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the importance of our work and their careful review. We address the issues raised by the reviewer in our point-by-point response below. Edits to the manuscript in response to the reviewer’s comments are highlighted in red in the revised manuscript.
Major Comments:
• The authors highlight repeatedly that in their analyses, although cells with identical TCRs are very close in gene expression space, gene expression differences between cells with different TCRs is unrelated to TCR similarity. This seems to be in strong contrast to reports showing that the TCR sequence can be predictive of T cell fate such as DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2024.115098, DOI: 10.1101/2025.05.31.657155, DOI: 10.1038/s41587-021-00989-2, DOI: 10.1038/s41590-022-01129-x. This apparent discrepancy needs to at least be extensively discussed, and preferably explained, in the current manuscript.
We thank the reviewer for this question. This is an important point raised by the reviewers, and we have added a deeper discussion of the relationship between TCR sequence and T cell state, and how fate is shaped by TCR-intrinsic vs extrinsic factors. Briefly, the model raised by the reviewer is that T cells with similar TCR sequences have similar transcriptional programs because their TCRs have similar antigen specificity, signaling strength, and encounter similar tissue microenvironments that then drive convergence to similar functional states. As a counterpoint, even T cells with shared TCR sequences may diverge in their functional states due to TCR-extrinsic factors: variable antigen and cytokine exposure, variable costimulatory molecules, epigenetic plasticity, and stochastic cell fate bifurcations, e.g. one daughter T cell acquires a memory fate and the other an effector fate (DOI: 10.1016/j.coi.2009.05.021 and DOI: 10.1038/s41590-022-01337-5).
CoNGA was one of the first frameworks for systematically identifying correlations between TCR sequence and gene expression (DOI: 10.1038/s41587-021-00989-2). Interestingly, these correlations often highlighted unconventional T cells such as mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells and invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells, and the authors noted that successfully applying their method required a large number of clonotypes (100s) and an even larger number of T cells (10s of thousands). This observation is held up in the authors’ recent, more expansive effort metaCoNGA (DOI: 10.1101/2025.05.31.657155) that analyzed 6 M T cells across 91 studies. Again, the authors observed TCR-gene expression correlations in unconventional T cells (iNKT, MAIT, KIR+ CD8+ T cells), as well as in T cells with TCRs sharing the same target antigen. While significant, this was not a widespread correlation; only 9% of CD8+ and 2% of CD4+ T cell gene expression graph neighborhoods showed significantly similar TCR CDR3 sequences. So similarities in TCR sequence and antigen specificity do drive similar T cell fates, but this effect does not explain the majority of the T cell phenotypes.
In parallel work, Raychaudhuri et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41590-022-01129-x) identified TCR features that promoted the Treg cell fate and then developed a scoring system (TiRP) to predict cell fate (Treg or Tconv) based on those TCR features. They then expanded this work (DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2024.115098), using ML models and TCR biophysical features to define four TCR scoring functions that quantify T cell fates encoded by the TCR: “TCR-innate’” to predict the innate-like, PLZFhigh state, “TCR-CD8” to predict the CD8+ state, “TCR-reg” to predict the Treg cell state, and “TCR-mem” to predict the memory state. Consistent with the CoNGA work, the strongest relationships between TCR sequence and transcriptional cell fate were found in unconventional or very specific T cell subsets, like MAIT cells and KIR+ HELIOS+ CD8 T cells. The authors also acknowledged the contributions of TCR-extrinsic effects: the amount of variance in T cell state explained by the TCR is significant but modest considering the full diversity of the repertoire. For any given TCR, specific antigenic contacts and co-stimulatory signals are likely the major determinants of T cell phenotype.
To summarize, the above four works establish that TCR sequence provides information on both antigen specificity and transcriptional cell fate, but the effect is largest in unconventional T cells and still, TCR-extrinsic effects are the larger determinant of fate. Our study does not contradict these findings. Although we found little relationship between TCR sequence similarity and RNA expression–measured by Hamming distance or Levenshtein distance (see below)-- activated and expanded T cells clones with very different TCR sequences can present similar RNA expression profiles. We leveraged this relation to generate accurate RNA and TCR distributions across conditions, and extrapolate clonal expansion and gene expression for unseen patients or conditions. In response to the reviewer, we cover this seeming discrepancy in the discussion. A major contribution of our work is to also show that clonal expansion, derived from the TCR sequence, also informs T cell fate. We performed additional analysis to check our datasets for the presence of unconventional T cells, verifying lack of expression of marker genes TCRD, TCRG, and very low level of expression for RORC (Response Fig. 1).
Response Figure 1. Expression distribution of gene RORC in the HNSCC dataset.
In response to this comment, we added the following text to the Discussion: “We observed little relationship between cells’ similarity in their TCR sequences and their gene expression values, contrasting with reports that TCR sequences can predict T cell fate outcomes. T cells with similar TCR sequences may have similar transcriptional programs because their TCRs have similar antigen specificity, signaling strength, and encounter similar tissue microenvironments that then drive convergence to similar functional states. However, even T cells with shared TCR sequences may diverge in their functional states due to TCR-extrinsic factors: variable antigen and cytokine exposure, variable costimulatory molecules, epigenetic plasticity, and stochastic cell fate bifurcations [48,49]. Previous studies, including CoNGA, metaCoNGA, and a range of TCR scoring frameworks (TiRP, TCR-innate, TCR-CD8, TCR-reg, TCR-mem), systematically examined the relationships between TCR sequence and gene expression, and established that TCR sequence provides information on both antigen specificity and transcriptional cell fate [32,40,50,51]. However this effect was largest in unconventional T cells, which are not present in our data, and TCR-extrinsic effects were the larger determinant of T cell fate.”
• What is the rationale for using only the beta chain? Clarifying this choice would help assess how much signal is potentially missed by excluding the alpha chain.
We thank the reviewer for this question. A known experimental limitation of single cell V(D)J-Seq is that the TCR alpha and beta chains are not always paired, due to difficulty in capturing their transcripts in single cells. In a typical scV(D)J-Seq experiment (e.g., in the blood samples in PMID 35803260), 87% of cells have both the alpha and beta chain sequence recovered, and the beta chain is recovered at a higher frequency compared to the alpha chain (95% vs 89%). Across the largest TCR sequence databases, 94% of sequences contain only the beta chain (PMID 36755161). This is an area for further development as scV(D)J-Seq technology advances. In other publications that model both chains, performance increases, albeit marginally, and this is likely because the CDR3 beta sequence is the largest contributor in the TCR sequence to determining peptide-MHC interaction specificity (PMID 11696602, PMID 10542151).
We have added the following text to the second paragraph of Results section 1 to clarify this aspect: “We focus on the β chain for practical and biological reasons. First, in single-cell V(D)J sequencing, α–β pairing is often incomplete. In blood samples profiled in [19], 87% of cells have paired chains, with β recovered more frequently than α (95% vs. 89%). More broadly, large public TCR resources are predominantly β-only, with 94% of sequences containing only the β chain [41]. Second, prior studies that include both chains report only marginal performance gains, likely because the CDR3β sequence is the dominant determinant of peptide–MHC specificity [42,43]. Given these experimental constraints and data availability, we use the β chain to maximize sample coverage while retaining most of the relevant signal.”
• Why was Hamming distance used for TCR similarity, whereas Levenshtein distance is more commonly adopted in TCR studies? Levenshtein allows exploration of amino acid-level mismatches that Hamming does not.
We thank the reviewer for raising this point. To address this concern, we repeated the analysis using Levenshtein distance instead of Hamming distance. The results are presented in two new figure panels (Extended Fig. 2b and Extended Fig. 4c) and are copied below in Response Figure 2 for convenience. We found that the findings remain consistent: Cells from the same clone (0-Levenshtein) are generally closer in RNA space. For non-clonal pairs, their relative positions in RNA space are approximately the same regardless of whether their TCRs differ by a single amino acid or by many.
Response Figure 2. Comparison of pairwise cell distances in RNA and TCR spaces via Levenshtein distances for the HNSCC dataset (Extended Data Fig. 2b) and the Pan-cancer dataset (Extended Data Fig. 4c)
• Performance on the pan-cancer dataset appears notably more modest than on HNSCC. This suggests potential limitations in generalization, and questions its contribution on a clinical perspective. Perhaps the difference comes from the source of healthy tissue (blood in HNSCC, juxta-tumor in pan-cancer). Can the authors identify another public dataset with blood and tumor (inline with the HNSCC cohort) to evaluate this possibility?
We thank the reviewer for this comment. This is an important point, and we agree that the source of healthy tissue (peripheral blood vs. normal adjacent tissue) is a potential confounder. To directly evaluate this possibility and assess the generalizability of TRIM, we have validated our model on a new, independent dataset as suggested. We identified a recent colorectal cancer (CRC) cohort from Chen et al. (2024, Cancer Cell, PMID 38981439), which, like our HNSCC cohort, includes paired single-cell RNA-seq and TCR-seq data from tumor tissue and peripheral blood samples, collected both before and after anti-PD-1 treatment.
We focused our analysis on 201,048 T cells from the tumor and peripheral blood samples among 22 patients. The corresponding results are reported in the new Extended Data Figures 3,7,10,14 and copied below. We first confirmed that this dataset exhibits the same core challenge as the HNSCC data: while T cells sharing identical TCR clones are closer in RNA expression space, the overall RNA-TCR distance correlations remain weak, even when using advanced TCR embeddings (Extended Data Fig. 3b-c). This reinforces the broad applicability and necessity of our pseudoclone framework.
We then evaluated TRIM's performance on this new CRC dataset with the following results:
1. Model fidelity: The model's outputs in RNA space closely matched the ground truth data. We observed a high correlation between real and predicted clonotype diversity (r = 0.67; Extended Data Fig. 7a-b) and strong agreement in clustering analysis across various resolutions (r = 0.94, 0.85, and 0.86 for k = 10, 25, and 50, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 7c).
2. Clinical relevance (clonal expansion): In a leave-one-patient-out evaluation, TRIM demonstrated strong predictive power, achieving an AUC of 0.83 for predicting post-treatment clonal expansion. In contrast, baseline models (KNN and MLP) performed worse than or near random (Extended Data Fig. 10a-d).
3. Clinical relevance (gene identification): The model also excelled at identifying differentially expressed genes associated with clonal expansion in a leave-one-out evaluation, achieving an AUC of 0.85 for all T cells (0.82 for CD4 and 0.79 for CD8 cells; Extended Data Fig. 14a).
We consider these results strong given that this CRC dataset introduces greater temporal complexity than the HNSCC dataset. In the new dataset, treatment timepoints span a larger timeframe compared to the HNSCC dataset (up to 250 days vs. 14 days from treatment start). To boost the signal, we aggregated the "on-treatment" measurements from the source study as our "post-treatment" timepoint (Methods). This longer time span and necessary aggregation introduce significant additional heterogeneity, which likely accounts for the slight difference in the clonal expansion metric (AUC = 0.83 in CRC vs. AUC = 0.92 in HNSCC). However, in both cohorts, baseline models performed at best near random. In summary, we believe these results on a new, clinically relevant dataset that matches the tissue-sourcing criteria (tumor and peripheral blood) supports the model's generalizability across different cancer types, and its potential clinical contribution.
We have added the following paragraphs to the Results section to describe this new analysis and its findings. The new Extended Figures are also provided.
● Results section 2: “In addition, we investigated another dataset containing paired single-cell RNA-seq and TCR-seq data from 20 colorectal cancer (CRC) and 2 duodenal cancer patients [27]. This dataset includes samples from tumor tissue, adjacent normal tissue, and peripheral blood collected before and after anti–PD-1 treatment. For consistency with our main analysis, we focused on tumor and peripheral blood samples and restricted the analysis to T cells with paired RNA-seq and TCR-seq (Extended Data Fig. 3a, Methods). This resulted in 201,048 T cells with RNA expression profiles measured across 36,027 genes, each paired with a corresponding TCR CDR3 β-chain sequence. As in the HNSCC dataset, T cells sharing identical TCR clones were closer in RNA expression space than random cell pairs (Extended Data Fig. 3b). Furthermore, RNA–TCR distance correlations remained weak even when using TCR-BERT or CNN autoencoder embeddings (Extended Data Fig. 3c), reinforcing the broader applicability of our pseudoclone framework and model.”
● Results section 3: “We then evaluated TRIM on the CRC dataset to assess its generalizability. The model outputs in RNA space closely matched the ground truth, and the correlation between real and predicted clonotype diversity was high (r = 0.67; Extended Data Fig. 7a-b). A more detailed clustering analysis also demonstrated strong agreement between real and generated data, with high correlations in median TCR clone counts across clustering resolutions (r = 0.94, 0.85, and 0.86 for k = 10, 25, and 50, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 7c).”
● Results section 4: “Similarly, we evaluated TRIM on the CRC dataset. In leave-one-out evaluation, TRIM achieved an AUC of 0.83 for predicting post-treatment clonal expansion, whereas baseline models (KNN and MLP) performed worse than or near random (even after extensive greedy hyperparameter optimization) regardless of whether they used RNA expression, TCR embeddings, or their combination as input (Extended Data Fig. 10a-d, Methods).”
● Results section 5: “We then evaluated TRIM’s ability to identify differentially expressed genes on the CRC dataset. In leave-one-out evaluation, TRIM achieved AUC of 0.85 for all T cells, 0.82 for CD4 cells, and 0.79 for CD8 cells (Extended Data Fig. 14a).”

In the source study, “pre-” and “post-treatment” correspond to baseline and on-treatment visits. Because some patients had multiple on-treatment samples, we aggregated those measurements at the patient level for each condition to make full use of the data.”

• Page 10, towards the end of last paragraph “When we isolated this subset of genes in our model’s ranking by log fold change, we found that, as expected, the expansion signature genes were more likely to be differentially expressed in clones that the model predicted to expand (Fig. 5a).” : Given that the p value for this test is 0.064, I do not understand why it is described as a positive result.
We thank the reviewer for this question. We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern and agree that the phrasing could be misleading. Our intent was to emphasize the observed trend, rather than to claim a statistically significant result. We hypothesize that this signal is attenuated—and thus fails to reach full statistical significance—because the expansion signatures were derived from tumor tissue, while our analysis was modeling expansion in peripheral blood. Finding a positive trend in this cross-compartment comparison aligns with prior evidence that tumor-associated expansion programs are indeed detectable, if more weakly, in circulation.
We have revised the text to accurately reflect this, describing it as a "positive trend" rather than a significant finding: “When we restricted our analysis to these genes and ranked them by log-fold change, expansion-signature genes were more likely to be up-regulated in clones the model predicted to expand (Fig. 5a). Quantification using a Wilcoxon rank sum test [45] for the hypothesis whether the model ranks the expansion signature genes higher than the non-expansion signature genes resulted in a p-value of 0.064. Because the signatures were derived from tumor tissue whereas our analysis models expansion in blood, we expect some attenuation; nonetheless, the result shows a directionally consistent enrichment and aligns with prior evidence that tumor-associated expansion programs are detectable in blood.”
Minor Comments:
• Consider comparing TCR-derived distances to those in the gene expression PCA space as a control of model latent space structure (and deformation).
We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. To clarify, this comparison was already performed in our analysis and is presented in Figure 3C, where we compared the TCR-derived distances with those from the gene expression PCA space. We have added a clarification in the legend of Fig. 3c: “Plots showing no relationship in non-clones between their pairwise distance in RNA space (computed in the RNA PCA space using the first 100 principal components) and their pairwise TCR distance, using either TCR-BERT embeddings or our CNN-based autoencoder embeddings.”
• How do VDJ gene usages structure the TCR space? This could provide insight into how biologically meaningful the learned representations are, and also how just using these information could be sufficient for the model.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. We do not explicitly use V, D, and J gene segment information in our model, and instead use the CDR3 sequences from the β chains, which implicitly contain full information on the D segment, and partial information on the V and J segments. We have clarified this further in the Methods section: “The TCR representations used in TRIM are based on the trained embeddings obtained from a CNN autoencoder that we learned in a pre-processing step. For each TCR, its CDR3 β chain sequence was input to the model as a null-padded sequence of amino acids, with each amino acid encoded using its corresponding Atchley factors.”
Previous studies have established that including V/J gene segment information results in a richer TCR representation that improves performance on supervised prediction tasks (PMIDs 38070156, 33707415, 37556545), and that the frequency of TRAV/TRBV gene segments is shaped by genetic variation in the MHC locus (PMID 27479906). In models from these studies, the CDR3β sequence is the largest contributor to performance. scV(D)J-Seq is somewhat limited in full identification of the V and J gene segments. Here, we have visualized how structured the TCR representations learnt by our CNN autoencoder are by the V and J gene segments experimentally available (Response Fig. 3). For clarity, we colored cells by the top 5 most abundant V and J genes in the β chain. The clusters of CDR3 sequences clearly tend to be represented by a smaller number of V and J gene segments, indicating that these segments contribute to the TCR embedding structure and that our model implicitly learns about these segments through the CDR3β sequences.

• Figure 4A, for comparing real vs generated data patterns, it would be helpful to include a more quantitative analysis than the two UMAPs. Eg perhaps a clustering analysis or “contour line” visualization would be more informative.
We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and agree that a more quantitative comparison would strengthen this figure. We would like to clarify that we have performed a clustering-based analysis in Extended Fig. 6b, where we computed the median clone count per RNA cluster and reported the Pearson correlation between real and generated distributions. This turns the UMAP visualization into a quantitative summary across clusters. We have made the following clarification in the Results section: “To assess whether TRIM captures the structure of the RNA space, we performed a clustering analysis. Specifically, we clustered cells in RNA expression space using k-means (with k = 10, 25, and 50), calculated the median clone count in each cluster for both real and generated data, and then calculated the correlation between these values. In other words, we divided the RNA space into distinct groups and evaluated whether TRIM reproduced the corresponding patterns in TCR space. Across all clustering resolutions, the correlations were consistently high (r = 0.92, 0.95, and 0.92 for k = 10, 25, and 50, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 6b). ”
• Fig 4B and middle of first full paragraph on page 8 “We found that the true clonal diversity for each condition and the predicted pseudoclone diversity for that condition are strongly correlated (r = 0.80)” : Including other repertoire metrics like Shannon entropy could help quantify clonal diversity more robustly.
We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. We agree that adding Shannon entropy provides a more robust quantification of clonal diversity. Following this suggestion, we adopted the Shannon entropy as a measure of clonal diversity in all our analyses, and updated Figure 4b to feature this metric. We found that the true clonal diversity (measured by entropy) and the predicted pseudoclone diversity remain strongly correlated (r = 0.74). We moved our original analysis (using the fraction-unique metric, r = 0.80) to Extended Data Fig. 6c as a complementary validation. The new figure is attached below.
We have added the following description to the Results section: “We next examined the clonotype diversity captured by TRIM for each condition, quantified using Shannon entropy (Methods). The true clonal diversity and the corresponding predicted pseudoclone diversity were strongly correlated (r = 0.74; Fig. 4b). To further assess this relationship, we also measured diversity as the proportion of unique TCRs in each sample, calculated by dividing the number of distinct TCRs by the total number of cells. This alternative yielded a similarly high correlation between true and predicted values (r = 0.80; Extended Data Fig. 6c). ”
In addition, we have included the following text in the Methods section to clarify how Shannon entropy was computed: “Shannon entropy was used to quantify TCR clone diversity. For each sample, we identified all observed T-cell clones, counted the frequency of each unique clone, and converted these counts to probabilities by dividing by the total number of observations. Entropy was then calculated as H = -∑ p log p, where p represents the probability of clone i.”

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The study reported TRIM as a promising tool for predicting T cell states and responses to cancer immunotherapies using peripheral blood measurements. While the initial findings are encouraging and highlight the potential for clinical application, there are several areas that warrant further clarification and expansion to enhance the study's impact and translational relevance.
Major comments:
1. The study would be strengthened by a more in-depth analysis of inter-individual variability in immune responses. Key factors such as age, sex, race, and genetic background are known to significantly impact immune cell behavior and responses to immunotherapy. It remains unclear whether TRIM accounts for these sources of variation or how its predictive performance may differ across diverse patient populations. Including data analysis based on clinicopathological features in the patient cohorts would provide a more comprehensive assessment of TRIM’s potential for equitable application in clinical practice.
We thank the reviewer for this comment and agree with the reviewer that inter-individual variability in immune responses is an important consideration, and that factors such as age, sex, and genetic background play a significant role in shaping clinical outcomes. Given the limited nature of available single-cell TCR-RNA-seq clinical datasets, we designed TRIM around a leave-one-out evaluation strategy across patients, which is the most effective way to assess generalization under these data constraints.
To test the robustness of TRIM across different patient subgroups stratified by clinicopathological features, we conducted a new series of analyses based on the features available in a new colorectal cancer (CRC) dataset, which includes both tumor tissue and peripheral blood samples pre and post PD1-blockade with paired scRNAseq and scTCRseq.
We would like to note that this metadata is limited in the source publications: the HNSCC dataset did not release patient metadata, while the CRC dataset provided information on patient age and sex.
Using the available age and sex data from the CRC dataset, we performed a series of leave-group-out (LGO) analyses to test TRIM’s robustness. This involved holding out specific patient subgroups from training and evaluating the model's performance on them. We created subgroups for:
1. All female patients
2. Younger patients (defined as the lowest 15th percentile of the age distribution)
3. Older patients (defined as the highest 15th percentile of the age distribution)
(We noted that a 'leave-male-out' analysis was not feasible, as the small number of female patients was insufficient for robust model training (Extended Data Fig. 8a)).
In a similar LGO framework (and to address Reviewer Comment 5), we also tested TRIM’s robustness to a key technical variable: the number of cells sequenced per patient. We created subgroups for patients with few cells (lowest 15th percentile) and many cells (highest 15th percentile). At the same time, we acknowledge that the small sample sizes inherent to single-cell clinical studies place limitations on the statistical power of such subgroup analyses. These are limitations present in the original single-cell studies, which largely do not address inter-individual variability (PMIDs 35803260, 38981439).
● Robust generalization: Across these different conditions, TRIM consistently captured the joint RNA–TCR space at the distribution level, as indicated by high correlations across multiple clustering resolutions (k = 10, 25, and 50; Extended Data Fig. 8b–f).We observed that higher-resolution clustering makes predicting median TCR clone counts more challenging, and this difficulty is further amplified when evaluating samples with few cells, as smaller clusters contain very limited information for accurate estimation. However, TRIM maintained strong performance in predicting clonotype diversity, with high correlations between real and predicted values (Extended Data Fig. 8b–f, right panels). We did observe reduced generalizability when older patients were left out of training. This difficulty in generalization appears linked to distinct properties of these patients’ immune repertoires.
● Expansion prediction: We further tested TRIM’s ability of expansion prediction in leave-group-out settings, where the test patients had post-treatment measurements. TRIM maintained competitive performance, achieving AUCs of 0.68, 0.81, and 0.78 for leave-female-out, leave-young-out, and leave-more-cells-out evaluations, respectively, while baseline models again performed near random (Extended Data Fig. 11).
● We similarly evaluated TRIM’s ability to identify differentially expressed genes in the CRC dataset. Across different subgroup analyses, TRIM maintained strong performance, with AUCs for all T cells of 0.83, 0.90, and 0.81 for leave-female-out, leave-young-out, and leave-more-cells-out, respectively; for CD4 cells, 0.83, 0.83, and 0.81; and for CD8 cells, 0.72, 0.84, and 0.72 (Extended Data Fig. 14b-d).
These results provide a more comprehensive assessment of TRIM’s performance across different patient conditions, and further validate TRIM’s ability to generalize to different cancer types as well as across diverse patient conditions. 2. In this study, the authors applied TRIM to T cells isolated from both blood and tumor biopsies of patients with HNSCC. However, the rationale behind selecting HNSCC as the disease model is not clearly explained.
We thank the reviewer for flagging this. To our knowledge, the HNSCC dataset on which we trained our model represents the first dataset that aligned with our specific experimental requirements: a multimodal dataset where T cells are profiled in blood and tumor tissue across multiple treatment timepoints. The number of such available datasets is still very small; 2 studies to our knowledge (PMIDs 35803260, 38981439). These datasets are challenging to collect in the clinic (requiring paired sampling of patient tissue and blood at multiple time points) and to process experimentally (requiring T cell isolation and joint RNA and TCR sequence profiling). However these datasets have enormous potential to inform patient diagnosis and treatment, and we expect the number of studies with this design to increase in the next few years, which is why we developed the TRIM model.
3. The patient data used to validate the predictive value of TRIM were all derived from relatively less prevalent cancer types, including HNSCC, ESCA, THCA, and UCEC. While these datasets provide initial support for TRIM’s utility, validation in more common and clinically impactful cancer types, such as breast and prostate cancer, would significantly strengthen the generalizability and translational relevance of the findings. Including such high-prevalence cancers for data validation is required to enhance the clinical applicability of the tool.
We thank the reviewer for this comment and agree with the reviewer that demonstrating our model’s performance on the major cancer types is important. Thus, we tested our model’s performance on a newly collected multimodal dataset in colorectal cancer (CRC) (PMID 38981439), one of the most common cancer types. Currently, there is no public data from breast or prostate cancer with the desired experimental design.
We focused our analysis on 201,048 T cells from the tumor and peripheral blood samples among 22 patients. The corresponding results are reported in the new Extended Data Figures 3,7,10,14 and copied below. We first confirmed that this dataset exhibits the same core challenge as the HNSCC data: while T cells sharing identical TCR clones are closer in RNA expression space, the overall RNA-TCR distance correlations remain weak, even when using advanced TCR embeddings (Extended Data Fig. 3b-c). This reinforces the broad applicability and necessity of our pseudoclone framework.
We then evaluated TRIM's performance on this new CRC dataset with the following results:
4. Model fidelity: The model's outputs in RNA space closely matched the ground truth data. We observed a high correlation between real and predicted clonotype diversity (r = 0.67; Extended Data Fig. 7a-b) and strong agreement in clustering analysis across various resolutions (r = 0.94, 0.85, and 0.86 for k = 10, 25, and 50, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 7c).
5. Clinical relevance (clonal expansion): In a leave-one-patient-out evaluation, TRIM demonstrated strong predictive power, achieving an AUC of 0.83 for predicting post-treatment clonal expansion. In contrast, baseline models (KNN and MLP) performed worse than or near random (Extended Data Fig. 10a-d).
6. Clinical relevance (gene identification): The model also excelled at identifying differentially expressed genes associated with clonal expansion in a leave-one-out evaluation, achieving an AUC of 0.85 for all T cells (0.82 for CD4 and 0.79 for CD8 cells; Extended Data Fig. 14a).
We consider these results strong given that this CRC dataset introduces greater temporal complexity than the HNSCC dataset. In the new dataset, treatment timepoints span a larger timeframe compared to the HNSCC dataset (up to 250 days vs. 14 days from treatment start). To boost the signal, we aggregated the "on-treatment" measurements from the source study as our "post-treatment" timepoint (Methods). This longer time span and necessary aggregation introduce significant additional heterogeneity, which likely accounts for the slight difference in the clonal expansion metric (AUC = 0.83 in CRC vs. AUC = 0.92 in HNSCC). However, in both cohorts, baseline models performed at best near random. In summary, we believe these results on a new, clinically relevant dataset that matches the tissue-sourcing criteria (tumor and peripheral blood) supports the model's generalizability across different cancer types, and its potential clinical contribution.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This study takes single cell RNA transcriptomic data and TCR data from blood and tumour and integrates them into a single low dimensional latent variable (coded as a Gaussian of specified mean and variance in a space of predetermined dimension), which can then be decoded so as to produce a generative model of transcriptional state and TCR. It adds to a growing body of literature which addresses integration of multimodal data. The model is used to investigate the relationship between TCR and transcription, and to predict population-level features as well as individual cell expansion in tumour and blood pre-and post- treatment , based on pretreatment blood alone.
I would summarise the most important findings as 1. Transcriptional state of T cells from the same clone are more similar to each other than to other clones, but for non-identical TCRs there is no relationship to transcriptional state. 2. The expansion potential of a TCR can be predicted from its pre-treatment transcriptional state (as shown in the original paper).
I was less convinced by the comparisons between TRIM and other ML approaches to prediction – its hard to directly compare, and to ensure that the other methods have been optimised at hyperparameter level.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. We agree completely that a fair comparison requires rigorous and transparent optimization of all methods. To address this, we have now added Extended Data Fig. 10 to explicitly and transparently detail our extensive hyperparameter optimization procedure.
As described in the updated figure legend and supplementary note 1, our procedure, performed on the new colorectal cancer (CRC) dataset, which includes both tumor tissue and peripheral blood samples pre and post PD1-blockade with paired scRNAseq and scTCRseq, ensures that each baseline was optimized for the task. Specifically, within each leave-one-patient-out (LOO) cross-validation fold, we performed an internal grid search:
1. The training patients (all except the one held-out test patient) were further split into an 80% internal-training set and a 20% internal-validation set, stratified by patient.
2. A grid search was performed over a pre-defined set of hyperparameters for both KNN and MLP models.
3. The hyperparameter set yielding the best AUC on the internal-validation set was selected.
4. A new model with these optimal parameters was re-trained on the entire LOO training set (all patients except the held-out test patient) and then evaluated on the held-out test patient.
The hyperparameter grids searched were as follows:
● K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN):
○ n_neighbors: [5, 10, 20, 50]
● Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP):
○ hidden_layer_sizes: [(400, 200, 100), (256, 128), (128,), (512, 256, 64)]
○ alpha: [0.0001, 0.001, 0.01]
○ learning_rate_init: [0.0001, 0.001, 0.01]
This full optimization was repeated for each LOO fold and for each input modality (RNA-only, TCR-only, and combined RNA+TCR).
Despite this extensive optimization, the baseline models performed near random for clonal expansion prediction, while TRIM achieved an AUC of 0.83 (Extended Fig. 10).
Finally, while we believe this rigorous comparison is important, we would also like to re-emphasize that, to our knowledge, TRIM is the first model uniquely designed for the generative task of predicting complex cellular states across both time points and tissue compartments (e.g., from pre-treatment blood to post-treatment tumor). This is a fundamentally different and more complex task than that addressed by the baseline classifiers.

I was also not completely convinced about the insights into the gene prediction section. Why do the authors think that prediction of genes driving expansion is better or more complete than using the actual differential gene expression profiles for those T cells which expand? Is the imposition of similar transcriptional profiles for the same clone somehow reducing the noise in some way?
We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. We apologize for the lack of clarity and have revised this section in the manuscript. Our intention is not to claim that our predictive gene set is "better or more complete" than a standard differential expression (DE) analysis. The reviewer is correct that a standard DE analysis, by comparing T cells that actually expanded to those that did not, is the established method for identifying the gene programs associated with an expanded state.
Our model addresses a different, and complementary, clinical and biological question. The goal of our gene analysis is twofold:
1. Model Interpretability: To demonstrate that our model's predictions are not a "black box," but are driven by biologically relevant gene programs. By identifying the genes most salient to the model's prediction of expansion, we show that it has learned meaningful biological signals.
2. Clinical Relevance: Our model is designed for a scenario where post-treatment samples are not available. A standard DE analysis is impossible in this "baseline-only" setting. The clinical utility of TRIM is to take a patient's pre-treatment sample and predict their post-treatment T cell dynamics.
Therefore, the genes we identify are not necessarily the same as those from a standard DE analysis. A post-treatment DE analysis identifies the results of expansion. In contrast, our model's salient genes represent predictive, upstream features present in the pre-treatment baseline state. These features may represent the potential for clonal expansion before that expansion ever occurs.
We have added the following clarifications in our Results section: “Although TRIM requires access to paired pre- and post-treatment data during training, once trained, it can be applied to new pre-treatment-only samples to identify gene programs associated with T-cell expansion. This capability provides both model interpretability—by demonstrating that its predictions are driven by meaningful biological signals—and clinical relevance, as it provides these predictive insights in a common clinical setting where post-treatment samples are unavailable.”
I wondered why patient id is encoded in the model? Surely id is a totally arbitrary field ? Why does its encoding need learning ?
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point, which highlights a key aspect of our model's design. The reviewer is correct that the patient ID itself (e.g., 'Patient 1', 'Patient 2') is an arbitrary label, and our model does not use this ID as a direct predictive feature.
We have clarified this in the manuscript. The patient ID is used only as a grouping key to aggregate a patient's baseline data (RNA-seq and TCR-seq in pre-treatment blood). As now explicitly stated in the 'Learning condition embeddings' subsection of the Methods, the model learns a single, patient-specific embedding vector from that patient's data.
This learned vector—which captures the patient's unique biological baseline—is what's used as the 'patient' condition, not the arbitrary ID. This allows the model to capture individual-specific variation. We have also added a clarifying sentence to the legend of Figure 2a to make this mechanism clear.
We added the following clarifications in the Methods section: “It is important to note that the model does not use the arbitrary patient ID as a direct feature. Instead, the patient ID serves as a grouping key. The model learns a patient-specific embedding vector by aggregating the pre-treatment blood-derived RNA and TCR data for that specific patient (as described above). This learned vector, which captures the patient’s unique biological baseline, is what is used as the patient-level condition.”
We further clarified this in Fig2. legend: “After learning the embedding vectors for the conditions with our condition-learning process by using condition ID as key to group features (bottom right, Methods), the encoders map them into the latent space as in a variational autoencoder.”
I am not convinced of the predictive features of the model – leave-one-out prediction from a single data set is not equivalent to validating in an independent cohort, even with the same treatment and/or cancer, let alone more broadly. And, at least to my understanding, the validation in a second data set involved re-learning the model with the second set of data. So its unclear how generalizable the models are.
We appreciate the reviewer's important point regarding generalizability. We agree that the gold standard would be to train a model on a vast collection of data that could then be applied directly to a new, independent cohort without retraining.
However, we believe the field is not at that stage yet, primarily due to the current scarcity and high cost of generating the necessary paired scTCR-RNA-seq clinical datasets. Our goal, therefore, is to demonstrate methodological generalizability: that the TRIM framework is not a "one-off" solution overfit to the HNSCC dataset, but a robust and general-purpose method that can be successfully applied to other complex, paired scTCR-RNA-seq datasets to yield strong, clinically relevant predictions. We envision the primary intended use of TRIM at this stage is for it to be trained on a new cohort to fill in missing experimental data within that specific cohort. For example, it could predict post-treatment outcomes for patients who only have pre-treatment samples, or impute missing timepoints or tissue sites. To our knowledge, TRIM is unique in its ability to make such predictions (T cell single-cell gene expression and clonal expansion) across time and tissues.
We have added the following text to the Discussion section: “While we recognize that a model trained on multiple cohorts, including a large variety of cancer types, could potentially be directly applicable to unseen cancer-type settings without retraining, given the current paucity of such datasets, we believe this is not currently achievable, nor the most accurate and cost-efficient strategy to address our problem at hand: being able to predict missing data in complex cohorts across time points and tissue-sites. No other computational method, to our knowledge, productively uses the RNA and TCR sequence to predict transcriptional states across tissues and time points; however, there are still many questions that the work presented here leaves open.”
To further support TRIM methodological generalizability, we validated it on a new, independent dataset.
Validation on an independent CRC Cohort
We identified a recent colorectal cancer (CRC) cohort from Chen et al. (2024, Cancer Cell, PMID 38981439), which, like our HNSCC cohort, includes paired single-cell RNA-seq and TCR-seq data from tumor tissue and peripheral blood samples, collected both before and after anti-PD-1 treatment.
We focused our analysis on 201,048 T cells from the tumor and peripheral blood samples among 22 patients. The corresponding results are reported in the new Extended Data Figures 3,7,10,14 and copied below. We first confirmed that this dataset exhibits the same core challenge as the HNSCC data: while T cells sharing identical TCR clones are closer in RNA expression space, the overall RNA-TCR distance correlations remain weak, even when using advanced TCR embeddings (Extended Data Fig. 3b-c). This reinforces the broad applicability and necessity of our pseudoclone framework.
We then evaluated TRIM's performance on this new CRC dataset with the following results:
7. Model fidelity: The model's outputs in RNA space closely matched the ground truth data. We observed a high correlation between real and predicted clonotype diversity (r = 0.67; Extended Data Fig. 7a-b) and strong agreement in clustering analysis across various resolutions (r = 0.94, 0.85, and 0.86 for k = 10, 25, and 50, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 7c).
8. Clinical relevance (clonal expansion): In a leave-one-patient-out evaluation, TRIM demonstrated strong predictive power, achieving an AUC of 0.83 for predicting post-treatment clonal expansion. In contrast, baseline models (KNN and MLP) performed worse than or near random (Extended Data Fig. 10a-d).
9. Clinical relevance (gene identification): The model also excelled at identifying differentially expressed genes associated with clonal expansion in a leave-one-out evaluation, achieving an AUC of 0.85 for all T cells (0.82 for CD4 and 0.79 for CD8 cells; Extended Data Fig. 14a).
We consider these results strong given that this CRC dataset introduces greater temporal complexity than the HNSCC dataset. In the new dataset, treatment timepoints span a larger timeframe compared to the HNSCC dataset (up to 250 days vs. 14 days from treatment start). To boost the signal, we aggregated the "on-treatment" measurements from the source study as our "post-treatment" timepoint (Methods). This longer time span and necessary aggregation introduce significant additional heterogeneity, which likely accounts for the slight difference in the clonal expansion metric (AUC = 0.83 in CRC vs. AUC = 0.92 in HNSCC). However, in both cohorts, baseline models performed at best near random. In summary, we believe these results on a new, clinically relevant dataset that matches the tissue-sourcing criteria (tumor and peripheral blood) supports the model's generalizability across different cancer types, and its potential clinical contribution.
We have added the following paragraphs to the Results section to describe this new analysis and its findings. The new Extended Figures are also provided.
● Results section 2: “In addition, we investigated another dataset containing paired single-cell RNA-seq and TCR-seq data from 20 colorectal cancer (CRC) and 2 duodenal cancer patients [27]. This dataset includes samples from tumor tissue, adjacent normal tissue, and peripheral blood collected before and after anti–PD-1 treatment. For consistency with our main analysis, we focused on tumor and peripheral blood samples and restricted the analysis to T cells with paired RNA-seq and TCR-seq (Extended Data Fig. 3a, Methods). This resulted in 201,048 T cells with RNA expression profiles measured across 36,027 genes, each paired with a corresponding TCR CDR3 β-chain sequence. As in the HNSCC dataset, T cells sharing identical TCR clones were closer in RNA expression space than random cell pairs (Extended Data Fig. 3b). Furthermore, RNA–TCR distance correlations remained weak even when using TCR-BERT or CNN autoencoder embeddings (Extended Data Fig. 3c), reinforcing the broader applicability of our pseudoclone framework and model.”
● Results section 3: “We then evaluated TRIM on the CRC dataset to assess its generalizability. The model outputs in RNA space closely matched the ground truth, and the correlation between real and predicted clonotype diversity was high (r = 0.67; Extended Data Fig. 7a-b). A more detailed clustering analysis also demonstrated strong agreement between real and generated data, with high correlations in median TCR clone counts across clustering resolutions (r = 0.94, 0.85, and 0.86 for k = 10, 25, and 50, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 7c).”
● Results section 4: “Similarly, we evaluated TRIM on the CRC dataset. In leave-one-out evaluation, TRIM achieved an AUC of 0.83 for predicting post-treatment clonal expansion, whereas baseline models (KNN and MLP) performed worse than or near random (even after extensive greedy hyperparameter optimization) regardless of whether they used RNA expression, TCR embeddings, or their combination as input (Extended Data Fig. 10a-d, Methods).”
● Results section 5: “We then evaluated TRIM’s ability to identify differentially expressed genes on the CRC dataset. In leave-one-out evaluation, TRIM achieved AUC of 0.85 for all T cells, 0.82 for CD4 cells, and 0.79 for CD8 cells (Extended Data Fig. 14a).”
● Methods: “Colorectal cancer dataset: This dataset is derived from the publicly available data from [27]. We used paired scRNAseq and scTCRseq data from 22 patients across 4 different conditions: blood pre-treatment, blood post-treatment, tumor pre-treatment and tumor post-treatment. In the source study, “pre-” and “post-treatment” correspond to baseline and on-treatment visits. Because some patients had multiple on-treatment samples, we aggregated those measurements at the patient level for each condition to make full use of the data.”

Robustness to Patient Subgroups
To test the robustness of TRIM across different patient subgroups stratified by clinicopathological features, we conducted a new series of analyses based on the features available in a new colorectal cancer (CRC) dataset, which includes both tumor tissue and peripheral blood samples pre and post PD1-blockade with paired scRNAseq and scTCRseq.
We would like to note that this metadata is limited in the source publications: the HNSCC dataset did not release patient metadata, while the CRC dataset provided information on patient age and sex.
Using the available age and sex data from the CRC dataset, we performed a series of leave-group-out (LGO) analyses to test TRIM’s robustness. This involved holding out specific patient subgroups from training and evaluating the model's performance on them. We created subgroups for:
4. All female patients
5. Younger patients (defined as the lowest 15th percentile of the age distribution)
6. Older patients (defined as the highest 15th percentile of the age distribution)
(We noted that a 'leave-male-out' analysis was not feasible, as the small number of female patients was insufficient for robust model training (Extended Data Fig. 8a)).
In a similar LGO framework (and to address Reviewer Comment 5), we also tested TRIM’s robustness to a key technical variable: the number of cells sequenced per patient. We created subgroups for patients with few cells (lowest 15th percentile) and many cells (highest 15th percentile). At the same time, we acknowledge that the small sample sizes inherent to single-cell clinical studies place limitations on the statistical power of such subgroup analyses. These are limitations present in the original single-cell studies, which largely do not address inter-individual variability (PMIDs 35803260, 38981439).

However, TRIM maintained strong performance in predicting clonotype diversity, with high correlations between real and predicted values (Extended Data Fig. 8b–f, right panels). We did observe reduced generalizability when older patients were left out of training. This difficulty in generalization appears linked to distinct properties of these patients’ immune repertoires.
● Expansion prediction: We further tested TRIM’s ability of expansion prediction in leave-group-out settings, where the test patients had post-treatment measurements. TRIM maintained competitive performance, achieving AUCs of 0.68, 0.81, and 0.78 for leave-female-out, leave-young-out, and leave-more-cells-out evaluations, respectively, while baseline models again performed near random (Extended Data Fig. 11).
● We similarly evaluated TRIM’s ability to identify differentially expressed genes in the CRC dataset. Across different subgroup analyses, TRIM maintained strong performance, with AUCs for all T cells of 0.83, 0.90, and 0.81 for leave-female-out, leave-young-out, and leave-more-cells-out, respectively; for CD4 cells, 0.83, 0.83, and 0.81; and for CD8 cells, 0.72, 0.84, and 0.72 (Extended Data Fig. 14b-d).
These results provide a more comprehensive assessment of TRIM’s performance across different patient conditions, and further validate TRIM’s ability to generalize to different cancer types as well as across diverse patient conditions. We hypothesize that this difficulty in generalization may be due to the distinct properties of this patients’ subpopulation, which shows reduced T cell clonal diversity. Nonetheless, the results across all subgroup analyses were consistent, indicating that TRIM is robust to demographic and sample-size variations.”

TRIM maintained competitive performance, achieving AUCs of 0.68, 0.81, and 0.78 for leave-female-out, leave-young-out, and leave-more-cells-out evaluations, respectively, while baseline models again performed near random (Extended Data Fig. 11).”
In Results section 5, we added: “Across different subgroup analyses, TRIM maintained strong performance, with AUCs for all T cells of 0.83, 0.90, and 0.81 for leave-female-out, leave-young-out, and leave-more-cells-out, respectively; for CD4 cells, 0.83, 0.83, and 0.81; and for CD8 cells, 0.72, 0.84, and 0.72 (Extended Data Fig. 14b-d). 1. The TRIM methodology is generalizable and highly effective on a new, independent, and more complex dataset.

In summary, the concept of TRIM is elegant and the fact that it is possible to encode the combined TCR/transcription profile in a low dimensional latent Gaussian variable and retain useful information is interesting. I am not convinced that the findings from application of the model so far substantially advance the field.
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the elegance of our model design and the strengths of our approach. We hope our additional analyses and clarification sufficiently demonstrate how our method's application can advance the field by generating predictions to fill in gaps in experimental data within complex cohorts of cancer patients receiving immunotherapies.

### Reviewer 1

He, C., Amodio, M. et al. introduces TRIM (TCR-RNA Integrating Model), a multimodal conditional variational autoencoder designed to jointly analyze T cell RNA and TCR sequence data. TRIM aims to learn a shared representation of transcriptomic and TCR clonality information, conditioned on key clinical and biological covariates such as patient identity, tumor vs other tissue, and treatment timepoint. The authors apply the model to two datasets: one comprising head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) patients sampled before and after checkpoint inhibition from blood and tumor, and another consisting of a pan-cancer RNA-TCR dataset with tumor and normal-juxta tissue. The model demonstrates predictive capabilities for T cell clonal expansion and transcriptional states, highlighting its potential utility in modeling T cell responses under treatment.
The study is timely and introduces a new approach for integration of these single-cell data modalities. The manuscript is clearly motivated, and the proposed method shows promising results in the field of immunotherapy outcome predictions. However, several aspects of the methodology and evaluation require clarification or expansion. Below, I provide detailed major and minor comments that could strengthen the manuscript.
Major Comments:
• The authors highlight repeatedly that in their analyses, although cells with identical TCRs are very close in gene expression space, gene expression differences between cells with different TCRs is unrelated to TCR similarity. This seems to be in strong contrast to reports showing that the TCR sequence can be predictive of T cell fate such as DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2024.115098, DOI: 10.1101/2025.05.31.657155, DOI: 10.1038/s41587-021-00989-2, DOI: 10.1038/s41590-022-01129-x. This apparent discrepancy needs to at least be extensively discussed, and preferably explained, in the current manuscript.
• What is the rationale for using only the beta chain? Clarifying this choice would help assess how much signal is potentially missed by excluding the alpha chain.
• Why was Hamming distance used for TCR similarity, whereas Levenshtein distance is more commonly adopted in TCR studies? Levenshtein allows exploration of amino acid-level mismatches that Hamming does not.
• Performance on the pan-cancer dataset appears notably more modest than on HNSCC. This suggests potential limitations in generalization, and questions its contribution on a clinical perspective. Perhaps the difference comes from the source of healthy tissue (blood in HNSCC, juxta-tumor in pan-cancer). Can the authors identify another public dataset with blood and tumor (inline with the HNSCC cohort) to evaluate this possibility ?
• Page 10, towards end of last paragraph “When we isolated this subset of genes in our model’s ranking by log fold change, we found that, as expected, the expansion signature genes were more likely to be differentially expressed in clones that the model predicted to expand (Fig. 5a).” : Given that the p value for this test is 0.064, I do not understand why it is described as a positive result.
Minor Comments:
• Consider comparing TCR-derived distances to those in the gene expression PCA space as a control of model latent space structure (and deformation).
• How do VDJ gene usages structure the TCR space? This could provide insight into how biologically meaningful the learned representations are, and also how just using these information could be sufficient for the model.
• Figure 4A, for comparing real vs generated data patterns, it would be helpful to include a more quantitative analysis than the two UMAPs. Eg perhaps a clustering analysis or “contour line” visualization would be more informative.
• Fig 4B and middle of first full paragraph on page 8 “We found that the true clonal diversity for each condition and the predicted pseudoclone diversity for that condition are strongly correlated (r = 0.80)” : Including other repertoire metrics like Shannon entropy could help quantify clonal diversity more robustly.
• Extended Fig 6C and end of last full paragraph on page 8 “Furthermore, the model also learned to match pseudoclone count in each region of the RNA space to the corresponding ground truth clone count for that region (Extended Data Fig. 6c, right plots). Together, these results indicate that the model achieves strong accuracy at both the dataset and cluster levels.” : Consider including more quantitative metrics of “accuracy” beyond clonal expansion and UMAP visualization, such as Euclidean distance in PCA space based on TRIM embedding or directly in TRIM latent space.
• Clone count distribution should be shown at the dataset level for both real and generated data to assess the generative model’s ability to reproduce this distribution.
• UMAP: It is unclear which embedding is being visualized, TRIM’s latent space or the gene expression PCA? This needs clarification at the beginning of the paper or in the Methods.
• Page 6 4th line of 2nd full paragraph, page 7 middle of first full paragraph, and page 12 5th line from top use the word “significantly” but it’s not clear a statistical test has been performed. Please clarify with details of the test or choose a different word.
• The list of genes identified across different methods in Figure 5 should be made available as supplementary material to enhance transparency and reproducibility.
• Is the scRNA-seq data log-transformed before analysis? This detail should be stated explicitly.
(Remarks on code availability)
I verified that the github page exists but I did not try installing or running the code. From my brief look, it seems this code is only to reproduce the figures of the manuscript, not to actually run the model on new datasets

### Reviewer 2

The study reported TRIM as a promising tool for predicting T cell states and responses to cancer immunotherapies using peripheral blood measurements. While the initial findings are encouraging and highlight the potential for clinical application, there are several areas that warrant further clarification and expansion to enhance the study's impact and translational relevance.
Major comments:
1. The study would be strengthened by a more in-depth analysis of inter-individual variability in immune responses. Key factors such as age, sex, race, and genetic background are known to significantly impact immune cell behavior and responses to immunotherapy. It remains unclear whether TRIM accounts for these sources of variation or how its predictive performance may differ across diverse patient populations. Including data analysis based on clinicopathological features in the patient cohorts would provide a more comprehensive assessment of TRIM’s potential for equitable application in clinical practice.
2. In this study, the authors applied TRIM to T cells isolated from both blood and tumor biopsies of patients with HNSCC. However, the rationale behind selecting HNSCC as the disease model is not clearly explained.
3. The patient data used to validate the predictive value of TRIM were all derived from relatively less prevalent cancer types, including HNSCC, ESCA, THCA, and UCEC. While these datasets provide initial support for TRIM’s utility, validation in more common and clinically impactful cancer types, such as breast and prostate cancer, would significantly strengthen the generalizability and translational relevance of the findings. Including such high-prevalence cancers for data validation is required to enhance the clinical applicability of the tool.
4. While the study identifies numerous genes and gene signatures through the application of TRIM, there is a lack of in- depth interpretation and biological context provided for these findings. Further analysis and discussion are needed to clarify the functional relevance of these genes, their potential roles in T cell biology or immunotherapy response,
5. It would be great to discuss on how sample size of patients contributes to the predictive power of the TRIM model.
(Remarks on code availability)

### Reviewer 3

This study takes single cell RNA transcriptomic data and TCR data from blood and tumour and integrates them into a single low dimensional latent variable (coded as a Gaussian of specified mean and variance in a space of predetermined dimension), which can then be decoded so as to produce a generative model of transcriptional state and TCR. It adds to a growing body of literature which addresses integration of multimodal data. The model is used to investigate the relationship between TCR and transcription, and to predict population-level features as well as individual cell expansion in tumour and blood pre-and post- treatment , based on pretreatment blood alone.
I would summarise the most important findings as 1. Transcriptional state of T cells from the same clone are more similar to each other than to other clones, but for non-identical TCRs there is no relationship to transcriptional state. 2. The expansion potential of a TCR can be predicted from its pre-treatment transcriptional state (as shown in the original paper).
I was less convinced by the comparisons between TRIM and other ML approaches to prediction – its hard to directly compare, and to ensure that the other methods have been optimised at hyperparameter level. I was also not completely convinced about the insights into the gene prediction section. Why do the authors think that prediction of genes driving expansion is better or more complete than using the actual differential gene expression profiles for those T cells which expand Is the imposition of similar transcriptional profiles for the same clone somehow reducing the noise in some way?
I wondered why patient id is encoded in the model? Surely id is a totally arbitrary field ? Why does its encoding need learning ?
I am not convinced of the predictive features of the model – leave-one-out prediction from a single data set is not equivalent to validating in an independent cohort, even with the same treatment and/or cancer, let alone more broadly. And, at least to my understanding, the validation in a second data set involved re-learning the model with the second set of data. So its unclear how generalizable the models are.
In summary, the concept of TRIM is elegant and the fact that it is possible to encode the combined TCR/transcription profile in a low dimensional latent Gaussian variable and retain useful information is interesting. I am not convinced that the findings from application of the model so far substantially advance the field.
(Remarks on code availability)
I did not have time to install adn test teh code on an HPC.
